sweep_summary: The search of works with stress or accent in the title for Mende (mend1266, catalog 'tonal', deciding source Dwyer 1978 'What sort of tone language is Mende?' SAL 9(2)) turned up one item: Dwyer 1978 'Idiosyncratic, suprasegmental processes in Mende', SAL 9(3):333-343 (Glottolog's 331-391 pagination is wrong). I downloaded the open full-issue PDF from journals.flvc.org, text in, logged) and read the article (pp. 95-105). It is a tone-only autosegmental study (high-falling tone pattern from apocope/syncope, demorphologized compounds, tonal/segmental parity, the definite suffix -i) and contains no statement about word stress or accent placement; a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence terms over the article returns nothing. It confirms the 'tonal' coding and does not supersede the catalog's deciding source. Nothing remains to acquire from this search of works with stress in the title (priority none); our earlier reading's list of works to obtain (Innes 1962/1971, Aginsky 1935, Conteh et al. 1983, Toda 1989) is unchanged.

new_statements.quote: In my paper read before the conference on African linguistics in Gainesville [Dwyer 1976], I claimed that Mende was not a suprasegmental tone language of the type envisioned by Leben [1973]. Yet, in that paper I suggested that there were a number of processes in Mende which nevertheless appeared to be of a suprasegmental nature. ... Mende contains a small set of disyllabic morphemes that display a high-falling tone pattern. ... Because examples of this tonal pattern are few in number and because this pattern is not present in Proto Southwestern Mande, the high-falling tone pattern appears to be a fairly recent development in Mende.
new_statements.citation: Dwyer, David J. 1978. "Idiosyncratic, suprasegmental processes in Mende." Studies in African Linguistics 9(3):333-343.
new_statements.reading: A specialist tonology paper that describes Mende word prosody entirely in terms of lexical tone melodies (H HL, L H L) associated to syllables, with no word-stress or accent statement anywhere. It confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding but adds nothing on stress; it is the companion to, not a replacement for, the catalog's deciding source (Dwyer 1978, SAL 9(2), which addresses the type of tone language directly).

new_statements.relation_note: Contradicts the catalog's tonal-only coding on its face (it states a fixed-penultimate accent with a final shift in definite nouns), but it is a 1908 phrasebook grammar written before Mende tone was recognised (Spears 1967, Dwyer 1978, Leben and the whole later literature describe Mende as a lexical-tone language). It should be recorded as a historical 'accent' statement, not as evidence for word stress; its penult/final pattern is consistent with the H(L) tone melodies later described.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A colonial-era, pre-tonological description: word 'accent' falls on the penultimate syllable; when a noun takes the definite singular suffix -i the accent moves to the last syllable; a few lexical exceptions are marked (e.g. the continuous-mood form tewema is said to carry the accent on the first syllable throughout, p. 87). Migeod never mentions tone, so his 'accent' is almost certainly the auditory impression of the H tone / HL melody, not a stress system.
new_statements.exceptions: 'The very few exceptions are specially marked'; definite singular nouns shift accent to the final syllable; tewema 'cutting' accented on the first syllable (p. 87)

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's 'tonal' coding (Dwyer 1978) and adds an instrumental observation: no stress-conditioned lengthening of the first syllable in Mende HL words and only slight, pitch-driven prominence on V1. It does not support Migeod 1908's pre-tonological 'penultimate accent' as a stress rule, but it does not address it either (disyllables only, where penult = first syllable).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mende (Sierra Leone; speaker of Kpa/'Kupa' Mende) is treated as a lexical tone language with the melodies H, L, HL, LH, LHL; in HL disyllables the first and second vowels take about equal shares of the word's duration (24% and 25%), unlike Daishan Wu where first-syllable stress lengthens V1 (44%); the author states that a stress effect 'is not the case' in Mende and that her impression of slight first-syllable prominence is attributable to the H pitch of the HL pattern. No word-stress rule is posited.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the Mende data are limited to HL disyllabic nouns from one speaker (groups AB [pOpO] 'representative', C [kenya] 'uncle', D [koba] 'lid')
new_statements.identity_note: Toda 1989's Mende data come from 'a young male native speaker of Kupa Mende' (= Kpa Mende, the western dialect of Sierra Leone Mende), recorded at ANU; the article's other language is the Daishan (Zhoushan) Northern Wu dialect of Chinese. Aginsky 1935 was based on speaker Dwight Sumner (Sierra Leone); Innes 1967 is standard (Kɔ) Mende of Sierra Leone. None concerns the Papua New Guinea Mende (mend1268).

tone_statements.quote: Downstep is a tonal phenomenon found in many West African languages, including Mende. ... Except for the presence of certain conflicting tonal alterations, Mende appears to be a classic example of such a step tone system. When these exceptions are viewed more closely, however, they provide much of the evidence for the conclusion that Mende does have a typical underlying two tone system.

tone_statements.summary: Two underlying level tones plus downstep (n, n-3, n+2 step rules); surface contours on morpheme-final cvv derived by Rule 9 'tone contouring'. 40+ tone-marked forms.

readall_conflicts: No new conflict. Toda 1989 (the one work opened) treats Sierra Leone Mende as a lexical tone language (H, L, HL, LH, LHL melodies) and reports, from one Kpa Mende speaker, no stress-conditioned lengthening in HL disyllables and only slight pitch-driven prominence on the first syllable; this is consistent with the catalog's 'tonal' coding (Dwyer 1978) and with Spears 1967. The standing disagreement held by the project is Migeod 1908's pre-tonological 'accent on the penultimate syllable, moved to the last syllable in the definite singular', which Toda neither confirms nor tests (her Mende data are HL disyllables only). Aginsky 1935 and Innes 1967/1971, both likely to discuss accent/tone explicitly, remain unopened (paywall / restricted deposit / lending only).

sources.quote: The OCP and UAC together produce the famous 5-way tone melody pattern of Mende (Leben 1973, 1978; Williams 1976) ... Mende exhibits surface tone melodies beyond the 5 canonical ones posited by Williams and Leben (Table 1), a point emphasized by Dwyer 1978. ... The 2,700 nouns in the Mende wordlist reveal many surface tone melodies.

tone.quote: Downstep is a tonal phenomenon found in many West African languages, including Mende. ... Except for the presence of certain conflicting tonal alterations, Mende appears to be a classic example of such a step tone system. When these exceptions are viewed more closely, however, they provide much of the evidence for the conclusion that Mende does have a typical underlying two tone system.
